30.7 High-Energy Astrophysical Neutrinos
Neutrinos are expected to be produced in hadronic interactions in a variety of astrophysical
objects. IceCube has reported a population of astrophysical neutrino events extending from tens
of TeV to beyond ten PeV [164, 173, 174]. Multimessenger observations of the flaring blazar TXS

There is also expected to be a neutrino flux produced in cosmic ray GZK interactions. Mea-suring this cosmogenic4 neutrino flux above 1018 eV would help resolve the UHECR uncertainties
mentioned above. One half of the energy that UHECR protons lose in photoproduction interactions
that cause the GZK effects ends up in neutrinos [177]. Heavier nuclei produce lower energy neutrinos
due to the lower energy of their constituent nucleons. The magnitude of the cosmogenic neutrino
flux depends strongly on the cosmic-ray spectrum at acceleration, the cosmic-ray composition,
the cosmological evolution of the cosmic-ray sources, and the energy of the Galactic-extragalactic

# UHECR energy threshold in the 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics

**Draft for qualified-scientist review. Not for citation until the reviewer has checked the section attribution in §3 below.**

## 1. Answer

| Item | Answer |
|---|---|
| Energy threshold defining UHECRs in the 2024 PDG Review | **E = 10^17 eV** (= 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV = 1.602176634 × 10^-2 J) |
| Inclusive or exclusive | **Exclusive — strict inequality, E > 10^17 eV** |
| Measurement uncertainty | None. The value is a stipulated convention, not a measured quantity; it is exact as written (10^17 eV, one significant figure as printed). |
| Sample size | Not applicable — no data are analysed; this is a bibliographic determination from one source document. |

Equivalent forms, all consistent with the source's own unit usage: 10^17 eV = 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV = 0.01602176634 J (1 eV = 1.602176634 × 10^-19 J, exact by the SI definition of the electron-volt).

## 2. Verbatim source text

**Primary quote (the definitional statement):**

> "An extensive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV) subatomic particles in the stratosphere and upper troposphere."

Source: S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), *Review of Particle Physics*, Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024), Sec. 36 "Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics", §36.2.1 "Atmospheric fluorescence detectors" (revised March 2024, L.R. Wiencke). PDF: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-particle-detectors-non-accel.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T12:03:24Z; sha256 prefix 92b8d56c8743).

**Corroborating sentence in the same section (exclusive phrasing, but a reach statement rather than a threshold):**

> "With energies extending beyond 10^20 eV, ultra high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are the highest energy subatomic particles known to exist."

Same source and locator as above.

**What the dedicated Cosmic Rays review (Sec. 30) says — note the absence of a definitional inequality:**

> "... This is a challenging task mainly due to the small flux, with less than 1 particle per km2 per year above 30EeV (see Fig. 30.1) ..."

> "The cosmic-ray spectrum observed at Earth (Fig. 30.1, with Fig. 30.7 high-lighting the highest energies) can be characterized by a series of power-law functions proportional to E^-γ with γ ∈ (~2.5, ~5.0) ..."

> "Cosmic rays are a population of energetic elementary particles and nuclei with a steeply falling, nearly power-law spectrum extending from a few MeV to tens of J per particle." (this last sentence from the Sec. 30 introduction as captured in the 2022 revision of the same review, https://pdg.lbl.gov/2022/reviews/rpp2022-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T12:03:19Z, sha256 prefix 14eb64b9c4a4; the 2024 PDF page is dated 19 September 2024)

Sources for the Sec. 30 quotes: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf and its mirror https://pdgweb.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf (both fetched 2026-11-23T12:03:20Z, sha256 prefix c8f0620d58d3).

## 3. Provenance caveat the reviewer must see

1. **The explicit inequality is not in Sec. 30.** The dedicated "Cosmic Rays" review (Sec. 30) uses the abbreviation UHECR without, in the text retrieved, attaching a numeric threshold to the definition. The only explicit numeric definition of "ultra high-energy" in the 2024 edition is the Sec. 36.2.1 parenthetical `E > 10^17 eV`. The answer above therefore rests on Sec. 36.2.1, not on Sec. 30. If the requesting party means strictly "Sec. 30 of the 2024 PDG", the honest answer is "Sec. 30 states no definitional threshold"; the value 10^17 eV is the 2024 PDG's own explicit definition elsewhere in the same edition.
2. **Sec. 30's numeric anchors are not definitions.** "above 30EeV" (3.0 × 10^19 eV) is a flux statement (< 1 particle km^-2 yr^-1), and "tens of J per particle" (≈ 10^20–10^21 eV, since 10^20 eV = 16.02 J) is a spectral-range statement. Neither is phrased as a definition, and neither should be quoted as one.
3. **"Beyond 10^20 eV" is a reach statement, not the threshold.** It is exclusive in form but describes the highest energies observed, not the lower bound of the class. It does not conflict with a 10^17 eV definitional threshold: 10^20 eV is 1000× higher.
4. **Section 30 revision date.** The 2024 Sec. 30 PDF page is headed "19th September, 2024". The author list captured in the fetched text is from the 2022 revision (J.J. Beatty, J. Matthews, S.P. Wakely); the reviewer should confirm the 2024 byline and revision date on the title page before quoting.

## 4. Internal consistency check of every number stated here

| Quantity | Value | Conversion check | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Threshold | 10^17 eV | = 10^17 / 10^15 = 100 PeV | yes |
| Threshold | 10^17 eV | = 10^17 / 10^18 = 0.1 EeV | yes |
| Threshold | 10^17 eV | = 10^17 × 1.602176634e-19 = 1.602176634e-2 J ≈ 0.016 J | yes |
| Sec. 30 flux anchor | 30 EeV = 3.0 × 10^19 eV | 3.0e19 / 1e17 = 300; i.e. 300× above the threshold, so "above 30 EeV" is a strict subset of "E > 10^17 eV" — no contradiction | yes |
| Sec. 36 reach statement | 10^20 eV | = 100 EeV = 16.02 J; matches "tens of J per particle" | yes |
| Flux normalisation | < 1 particle km^-2 yr^-1 | 1 km^2 = 10^6 m^2; unit conversion only, no arithmetic conflict | yes |

No stated figure in this memo exceeds or violates a bound set elsewhere in the memo. No uncertainty is attached to the threshold because none exists in the source; the only uncertainty is bibliographic (which section is authoritative), and it is disclosed in §3 rather than quantified as a number.

## 5. Independent cross-checks on the convention (flagged as not re-fetched in this session)

These are given so the reviewer can see where the PDG statement sits relative to community usage. **They were not retrieved by the harness in this session and must be verified against the primary text before use.**

- The Pierre Auger Observatory and Telescope Array literature conventionally takes UHECRs to begin at E ≈ 10^18 eV (1 EeV), i.e. one decade above the PDG Sec. 36 figure; this is a convention, not a definition, and it varies between papers (some use 10^17 eV, some 10^19 eV).
- The Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) cutoff is usually placed near 5 × 10^19 eV, which the PDG Sec. 30 text invokes qualitatively ("GZK interactions", cosmogenic neutrinos "above 10^18 eV").
- Consequence for the reviewer: the field has **no single settled numeric threshold**; the defensible, source-grounded answer to the question as posed is the PDG's own explicit parenthetical, 10^17 eV, exclusive.

## 6. How to report this downstream

- Report the threshold as **E > 10^17 eV (100 PeV; 0.1 EeV)**, exclusive.
- If a single-word verdict is required: **exclusive**.
- If the citation must point at the "Cosmic Rays" review specifically, report: *the 2024 PDG Cosmic Rays review (Sec. 30) does not state a definitional threshold; the 2024 PDG's explicit definition appears in Sec. 36.2.1 as E > 10^17 eV.*
- Full citation to carry with the number: S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024), Sec. 36.2.1; https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-particle-detectors-non-accel.pdf; accessed 2026-11-23.

*Draft prepared by the Research Scientist; requires review by a qualified scientist before anything is run or published.*

Asks: (1) the energy threshold defining ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) in the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review; (2) whether that threshold is inclusive (>=) or exclusive (>).

Document of record: Particle Data Group, *Review of Particle Physics*, Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024), chapter **30. Cosmic Rays**, written October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muniz (Santiago de Compostela U.), Z. Cao (IHEP Beijing), U.F. Katz (Erlangen U.), P. Mertsch (TTK, RWTH), C. Spiering (DESY, Zeuthen); chapter dated 19 September 2024 on the PDF. URL: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T12:08:41Z, sha256 c8f0620d58d3 (prefix as recorded by the retrieval harness).

## 2. Answer

- **Threshold: E = 10^18 eV (= 1 EeV).**
- **Verdict: exclusive.** The defining condition is read as E > 10^18 eV; a cosmic ray at exactly 10^18 eV would not be counted as a UHECR under that phrasing.

Caveat that must travel with the answer: the numerical value is grounded in the retrieved corpus, but the *verbatim PDG defining sentence* was not among the retrieved excerpts (see Sec. 3, row C). The attribution 'the PDG review states 10^18 eV' is therefore provisional pending the check in Sec. 7.

## 3. Evidence, verbatim

| # | Source (fetch, sha256 prefix) | Verbatim passage | What it establishes |

| A | arXiv:2502.11834 (2026-11-23T12:08:37Z, dd4de209e8b5) | "Ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are extremely energetic particles, with energies **exceeding 10^18 eV**, that travel through space and reach Earth." | Explicit numerical threshold, stated as a strict inequality. This paper cites the PDG chapter as ref. (13): "S. Navas, et al., Review of Cosmic Rays (2024) ... To be published in Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)". |
| B | UHECR2024 Telescope Array proceeding, INSPIRE (2026-11-23T12:08:39Z, 6f74bd77105f) | "The Telescope Array (TA) experiment is a hybrid observatory designed to study ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)." | Term used without a numeric threshold; supports usage, not the value. |
| C1 | PDG Cosmic Rays chapter (2026-11-23T12:08:41Z, c8f0620d58d3) | "UHECRs are subject to the GZK effect, the energy loss of protons and heavier nuclei ... at energies above ' 50 EeV [153]." | Uses UHECRs as an existing category at 50 EeV; not a definition. |
| C2 | same | "... a large-scale dipolar anisotropy at energies above 8EeV with 6.9 sigma significance [154]. The amplitude of the dipolar anisotropy is d = 0.073 +0.010 -0.008 ... evidencing the extra-galactic origin of UHECRs above this energy threshold." | 8 EeV is an **anisotropy** threshold, not the UHECR definition. **Do not report 8 EeV as the answer.** |
| C3 | same | "... invisible energy that amounts to ~10%-20% of the shower energy for energies above 0.1 EeV ..." | Shower-physics statement at 10^17 eV; not a definition. |
| C4 | same | "For charged CRs, the energies extend from tens of MeV to close to 1 ZeV ..." | Total range only (1 ZeV = 10^21 eV). |

Row C is the honest weak point: **none of the retrieved PDG excerpts contains a sentence of the form 'UHECRs are defined as ... with energy above X'.** The 10^18 eV value is therefore reported as the convention the review operates with, explicitly written out in a paper that cites the review (row A), and consistent with every PDG usage retrieved (Sec. 5).

## 4. Why 'exclusive', and what the verdict does and does not mean

1. **Linguistic basis.** Both retrieved statements of the threshold use strict-inequality wording: "exceeding 10^18 eV" (row A) and the review's own habitual "above ... EeV" construction (rows C1, C2). 'Above' and 'exceeding' exclude the endpoint.
2. **Operational meaning.** Cosmic-ray energy is a continuously reconstructed quantity with finite resolution; no observatory can classify an event as sitting exactly on 10^18.000... eV. The inclusive/exclusive distinction at the boundary is a bookkeeping convention with no physical consequence, and the UHECR spectrum is continuous across it.
3. **What would flip it.** A verbatim PDG sentence reading '>= 10^18 eV', '10^18 eV and above', or 'of order 10^18 eV and higher' would make the verdict inclusive. See Sec. 7.
4. **Uncertainty and sample size.** A definitional threshold carries **no uncertainty and no sample size**; none is attached above. This is distinct from measured quantities quoted in the same review, e.g. the dipole amplitude d = 0.073 +0.010/-0.008 at 6.9 sigma above 8 EeV, which is a measurement with a stated uncertainty; the retrieved excerpt does not state the sample size behind it, so none is reported.

## 5. Unit conventions and internal consistency check

1 EeV = 10^18 eV; 1 PeV = 10^15 eV; 1 ZeV = 10^21 eV. Every figure that appears in this note was checked against the 10^18 eV lower bound:

| Quantity | Value in eV | Relation to threshold | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|---|
| UHECR threshold (this note) | 1 x 10^18 eV | — | reference value |
| Dipole / anisotropy threshold (C2) | 8 x 10^18 eV | 8x threshold, above it | yes |
| GZK-horizon energies (C1) | 5 x 10^19 eV (50 EeV) | 50x threshold, above it | yes |
| GZK cutoff, cited in row A | 10^19.8 eV = 6.3 x 10^19 eV (63 EeV) | above it | yes |
| 'Invisible energy' statement (C3) | 1 x 10^17 eV (0.1 EeV) | below it; shower physics, not classification | yes |
| Top of CR range (C4) | ~1 x 10^21 eV (1 ZeV) | above it | yes |

No stated value in this note violates the threshold it sets.

## 6. Competing definitions (context only — none of these is the PDG answer)

| Convention | Threshold | Phrasing | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| This note / row A | 10^18 eV | 'exceeding 10^18 eV' | standard UHECR convention |
| Pierre Auger spectrum analyses | 2.5 x 10^18 eV | analysis threshold 'above 2.5x10^18 eV' | an analysis cut, not a definition (cited in row A's reference list, ref. [15]) |
| Telescope Array anisotropy | 57 EeV | 'greater than 57 EeV' | an anisotropy cut, not a definition |
| 'Extremely high energy' (EHE) | ~10^20 eV | separate category | must not be substituted for UHECR |

## 7. Verification step required before this answer is used (falsifiers)

Open Sec. 30 of https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf and locate the sentence that introduces 'UHECR'. Then:

- If it reads 'above / exceeding / > 10^18 eV' -> answer stands: 10^18 eV, exclusive.
- If it reads '>= 10^18 eV' or '10^18 eV and above' -> ask 2 flips to **inclusive**; ask 1 unchanged.
- If it gives a different number (e.g. 10^17 eV or 10^19 eV) -> ask 1 changes; re-check Sec. 5 consistency table.
- If the review defines UHECRs only by reference to a named experiment's convention -> the answer must be attributed to that convention, not asserted as the review's own definition.
- If no defining sentence exists at all in the chapter -> the correct report is 'the review uses the term without defining a threshold', and both asks should be re-labelled as blocked rather than answered.

## 9. Limitations for the reviewer

1. The retrieved PDG excerpts are partial; absence of the defining sentence among them is **not** proof of absence from the chapter.
2. Author attribution is inconsistent across sources: the chapter byline names Alvarez-Muniz et al.; row A's reference list names 'S. Navas, et al.' for the same 2024 review. Check which form the reviewer wishes to cite.
3. Version drift: PDG reviews are revised between editions; the 2024 chapter is dated 19 September 2024 and was written October 2023. Quote the edition, not 'the PDG review' generically.
4. This note answers a definitional convention, not a measurement; no confidence interval applies to the threshold itself.

HIGHLIGHTS OF THE 2024 EDITION OF THE REVIEW OF PARTICLE PHYSICS
All PDG data and review articles are available online at pdg.lbl.gov.
869 new papers with 2,717 new measurements
• 320 new measurements from LHC
experiments (ATLAS, CMS and LHCb).
• Extensive Higgs boson coverage from 231
new papers and 557 measurements with
latest results on mass, couplings, decay
width and branching ratios, plus searches
for other neutral and charged Higgs bosons.
• Supersymmetry: 36 new papers with 148
measurements with major exclusions.
• Top quark: 35 new papers provide latest
results on mass, coupling, and the discovery
of four top quark production at LHC.
• W mass: CDF published a new measure-ment of the W mass. It is more precise
than the world average at the time, but the
two results disagree. See comments in
Particle Listings and our W mass review
referencing the extensive studies done by
the LHC TeV MW working group.
• c-, b-hadron physics: 161 papers and 597
measurements provide world-best data on
lifetimes, mixing, CP violation, CKM
angles, and constraints on new physics.
• Neutrino Physics: 10 new papers with
measurements on neutrino mass, mixing,
and CP-violation.
• Meson resonances: Substantial improve-ments, including new cross particle fits
involving J/ψ(1S), ψ2S) and ηc(1S),
merging of π1(1400) and π1(1600) with
non-qq¯ quantum numbers into same node,
listing of complex pole positions when
available, and inclusion of recently observed
states. Several mesons now considered
established added to Summary Tables.
• New naming scheme for the many recently
discovered mesons and baryons with c or b
quarks that are not compatible with
conventional qq¯ or qqq structures. Listed in
“Other mesons” and “Exotic baryons”
sections.
120 reviews (most are revised)
• Major revision of Higgs Physics review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics.
• Major revision of Cosmic rays review, now
covering all components of cosmic rays
including neutrinos (which were previously
discussed in Neutrino Telescopes in Particle
Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics).
• Major revison of Large time-projection
chambers for rare event detection in
Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator
Physics.
• Major revision of Top Quark review
summarizes latest LHC results and
constraints on new physics from top quark.
• Major revision of Heavy Non-qq¯ Mesons
review follows new naming scheme for
states not compatible with qq¯ or qqq
structures.
• Semiconductor detectors section of Particle
Detectors at Accelerators review includes
recent developments.
• New section on goodness-of-fit tests and
expanded discussion of statistical tests in
Statistics review.
• Updated EWK fit in Electroweak Model
and Constraints on New Physics review.
• Semileptonic B Hadron Decays,
Determination of Vcb and Vub includes
latest results and discusses long-standing
issues with inclusive and exclusive
measurements.
• Updated cross section results in the
Neutrino Cross Section Measurements
review.
• Updated τ decay parameters and
branching ratio (BR) fits, including new
treatment of BR(a1(1260) → πγ).

verdict.summary:
VERIFICATION MEMO — UHECR ENERGY THRESHOLD IN THE 2024 PDG REVIEW OF PARTICLE PHYSICS (SEC. 30, 'COSMIC RAYS')
Draft for review by a qualified scientist before any use or publication. Status: asks 1 and 2 BLOCKED (see §5). No threshold value is asserted.

1. BOTTOM LINE
Neither ask can be answered honestly from the text that was retrieved and read. The retrieved text of the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review contains no sentence that defines ultra-high-energy cosmic rays by an energy threshold, and therefore contains no boundary wording whose inclusive/exclusive status could be classified. The widely used community convention (1 EeV = 10^18 eV, usually phrased 'above') is deliberately NOT substituted here: doing so would attribute to the PDG a statement the retrieved PDG text does not make. §6 records that convention in a fenced, explicitly non-authoritative box, for the requester's information only.

2. SOURCE TARGETED
S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), 'Review of Particle Physics', Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024); Chapter 30, 'Cosmic rays (rev.)'; file https://pdgweb.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf (retrieved 2026-11-23T12:12:27Z, sha256 c8f0620d58d3). Review dated 19 September 2024 in its running head; retrieved excerpts carry page markers '20 30. Cosmic Rays' and '25 30. Cosmic Rays', so the review is at least 25 pages and the excerpts sample only part of it. The 2024 edition's Highlights note a 'Major revision of Cosmic rays review, now covering all components of cosmic rays including neutrinos' — i.e. the review was restructured this edition, which is a further reason not to assume where a definition would sit.

3. EVIDENCE RETRIEVED (verbatim, PDF hyphenation preserved)
(a) 'In the energy range above ∼ 100PeV the fluorescence technique is used to determine the primary cosmic-ray energy, with the atmosphere where the EAS develops functioning as a calorimeter. In the two state-of-the-art experiments for UHECRs, the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array, a sub-sample of events is recorded simultaneously with the fluorescence (FD) and the surface detector (SD) arrays.'
    → Establishes: a technique change above ~100 PeV (= 10^17 eV), and that Auger and TA are called UHECR experiments. Does NOT establish: any energy at which cosmic rays become 'UHECRs'. The sentence presupposes the category and never defines it.
(b) 'More than 6600 sources have been found emitting gamma-rays in the Milky Way ... 43 of them have emission of gamma-rays above 0.1 PeV referred as PeVatrons ...'
    → A different, gamma-ray-source convention (0.1 PeV = 10^14 eV). Not a UHECR definition; must not be conflated.
(c) '... LHAASO-KM2A registered more than 140 photons with energies above 3 TeV ... the highest energy photon above 13 TeV ...' and the LIV discussion.
    → Gamma-ray thresholds, unrelated.
(d) Particle-listings footnote (rpp2024-list-other-particle-searches.pdf): '... upper bound on ultra high energy cosmic rays at Auger experiment: e.g. tau(X) < 4 x 10^22 yr for m(X) = 10^16 GeV.'
    → Uses the term; states no threshold.
(e) Chapter listing (astro-cosmo.html) and figure index (figures.html) confirm the review exists as Chapter 30 with Figs. 30.1–30.16, but carry no definitional text.
No other retrieved passage contains the string 'UHECR' in a defining construction.

4. WHY THIS DOES NOT SETTLE ASK 1, AND WHY ASK 2 CANNOT BE SPLIT OFF
(i) No retrieved sentence has the required form 'cosmic rays with energies above/at or above X are called UHECRs'. (ii) The one numeric boundary retrieved (~100 PeV) is attached to an instrument technique, not to a definition, and the immediately following clause treats 'UHECRs' as an already-known category. (iii) Inclusive vs exclusive is a property of a boundary statement; with no boundary statement there is nothing to classify. Physically the distinction is measure-zero (a cosmic ray at exactly X eV), so it can only ever be settled by the review's wording — which is precisely what is missing. Any verdict would therefore be an inference about the authors' intent, not a reading of their text.

5. WHAT WOULD LIFT THE BLOCK — VERIFICATION PROTOCOL (to be run against the full PDF, Sec. 30)
Step 1. Open rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf in full; note that only pages ~20 and ~25 were sampled above.
Step 2. Full-text search (case-insensitive) for: 'ultra-high-energy', 'ultrahigh-energy', 'UHECR', 'EeV', '10^18 eV', '10**18', '1 EeV', 'above 10', 'exceeding', 'defined as', 'conventionally'.
Step 3. Read the Introduction (likely §30.1) and any subsection headed 'Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays' or 'UHECRs' in full; also check the opening paragraph of the section discussing Auger/TA and the captions/axis labels of Figs. 30.7 (all-particle spectrum) and any composition/arrival-direction figures.
Step 4. Record verbatim: section number, page number, full sentence, and whether the energy appears as a number with units (eV/EeV) or only as a plotted axis.
Step 5. Classify with this decision table:
   - 'above X', 'greater than X', 'exceeding X', 'in excess of X' → EXCLUSIVE.
   - 'at or above X', 'X and above', '>= X', 'from X upwards' → INCLUSIVE.
   - Both forms used in different places, or no explicit form → report 'not stated / mixed' and quote both; do not pick one.
   - Definition present only implicitly (e.g. a section heading with a figure axis starting at X) → report the implicit anchor with the exact figure/axis wording and label the convention 'not stated in words'.
Step 6. If a definition is found, report it as the answer with the verbatim quote and page; if not, the block stands and the review should be cited as not defining the term in the text examined.
Recording format: {section, page, verbatim sentence, numeric value with units, boundary form, inclusive/exclusive}.

6. FENCED NON-ANSWER — EXTERNAL CONVENTION (NOT FROM THE PDG REVIEW; DO NOT CITE AS PDG)
The cosmic-ray community commonly takes UHECRs to be those with energies above 1 EeV = 10^18 eV, phrased exclusively ('above'), while some authors and some experiments use 10^19 eV and Auger/TA operationally report above ~10^18.5 eV. None of this was found in the retrieved PDG text. It is recorded only so the requester knows what a full-text check is likely to turn up, and it must be verified against the PDF before it appears in any deliverable.

7. UNITS, UNCERTAINTY, SAMPLE SIZE
A UHECR threshold is a definitional convention, not a measurement: it carries no statistical or systematic uncertainty, no confidence interval, and no sample size, and it should be quoted exactly as the review writes it (order-of-magnitude form, e.g. 10^18 eV, rather than a spuriously precise figure). Conversions used above and to be kept consistent: 1 PeV = 10^15 eV; 100 PeV = 10^17 eV; 1 EeV = 10^18 eV.

8. FALSIFIERS OF THIS MEMO'S FINDING
This memo's claim — that the retrieved PDG text does not define UHECRs by an energy threshold — is falsified by any one of: (a) a verbatim Sec. 30 sentence of the form 'UHECRs are ... energies above/at or above X'; (b) a glossary, table, or figure-caption entry in Sec. 30 assigning a numeric UHECR onset; (c) a subsection heading in Sec. 30 that introduces a numeric onset in its first sentence. Any of these should be reported with page and verbatim wording, and the block on asks 1 and 2 lifted accordingly.
